Patient demographics:
  age: 31
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Judge
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Vignette:
Kian, a 31-year-old married judge of South Eastern Asian descent, presented with symptoms consistent with post-traumatic stress following a devastating natural disaster three years prior. He carried himself with a quiet intensity, a trait he found increasingly difficult to maintain as the demands of his high-pressure profession clashed with an ever-present internal turbulence.

The typhoon had struck without much warning, a sudden, furious assault on his coastal hometown. Kian remembered the deafening roar of the wind, the way the old building he was in groaned and shuddered, and then the sickening lurch as a section of the roof collapsed. He had been lucky, escaping with only minor cuts, but the hours that followed were etched into his mind as a series of horrifying, vivid pictures: the sight of injured neighbors pulled from the rubble, the desperate cries for help, and the makeshift triage station in the town square. He could still see the pale, drawn faces, the bloodied bandages, and hear the frantic sirens of the few emergency vehicles that managed to navigate the debris-strewn streets. The pervasive, cloying smell of antiseptic mixed with damp earth and something metallic – blood, he later realized – had clung to everything.

In the years since, Kian found that these fragmented, visual memories would ambush him without warning. They weren’t just images; they were full sensory assaults, making him feel entirely transported back to those terrifying moments. He would suddenly taste the metallic tang in the air, feel the tremor of the ground, and hear the distant, wailing sirens as if they were right beside him. What frightened him most was the feeling that these moments were completely real, as if time had folded in on itself.

His daily life, once meticulously ordered, had become a minefield of triggers. Being a judge meant spending long hours in the courthouse, a building often frequented by cleaning crews whose disinfectants brought back the pungent, clinical odor of the makeshift hospital, leaving Kian feeling suddenly disoriented and hyper-alert. On days when the weather mirrored the oppressive humidity and heavy skies of the typhoon, a deep sense of dread would settle over him, making it hard to concentrate on the complex legal arguments before him. Perhaps the most jarring were the ambulances. Their piercing wail, a sound he heard almost daily from his chambers overlooking the city streets, would instantly plunge him back into the chaos of the disaster’s aftermath, the urgent flashing lights behind his closed eyelids.

To cope, Kian had developed a rigid set of rules for himself. He tried hard not to think about the typhoon, pushing away any intrusive image or sensation with fierce determination, believing that engaging with it would somehow open a floodgate he couldn't close. He also found himself increasingly avoiding going out, preferring the controlled environment of his home or office to the unpredictability of the outside world. Social invitations with his wife, even simple dinners with friends, became sources of anxiety, leading to quiet arguments and a growing distance between them. Even at home, true relaxation felt dangerous. The idea of letting his guard down, of allowing his mind to wander, filled him with an almost physical apprehension. He had come to believe that constant vigilance was the only way to protect himself from being caught off guard again, leaving him in a perpetual state of low-grade tension.

The cumulative effect of these strategies had left Kian exhausted, perpetually on edge, and increasingly isolated. His wife, worried by his withdrawal, had gently but firmly encouraged him to seek help. He sat in the therapy room, a man accustomed to presiding over the fates of others, feeling profoundly vulnerable, yet also desperate for some semblance of the peace he once knew. He hoped that by speaking about it, he might finally find a way to escape the prison of his past, but he was deeply afraid of what might happen if he stopped trying so hard to keep it all contained.
